From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Beauty Is in the Street: A Visual Record of the May 68 Uprising   
Editors Johan Kugelberg and Philippe Vermés  
Cover artist _Atelier Populaire_  
Language English  
Subject Art of the May 1968 events in France  
Published 2011 (Four Corners Books)  
Publication place United Kingdom  
Media type Print  
Pages 272  
ISBN9780956192837
_**Beauty Is in the Street: A Visual Record of the May 68 Uprising**_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-dd-1) is a 2011 book of posters produced by the _Atelier Populaire_ (Popular Workshop) in support of the May 1968 events in France. It was edited by Johan Kugelberg with Philippe Vermés and published in the United Kingdom by Four Corners Books in 2011.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-ind-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)
Posters in Paris in July 1968
The _Atelier Populaire_, who designed and printed the posters, were a group of Marxist artists and art students who occupied the École des Beaux-Arts during the wave of wildcat strikes in May 1968.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-ind-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3) Using a silk-screen printing press they produced thousands of posters at a time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3) They typically were printed on newssheet using a single colour, and use a simple iconography in which the factory represents the role of workers in society and the fist stands for solidarity and resistance (see right).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)

They comment on topics including the freedom of the press (see also Censorship in France), colonialism (see also French colonial empire) and the status of immigrant workers (see also Immigration to France).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-eye-4) The posters were also used to voice opposition to consumerism and were inspired by the Situationist International's critique of the spectacle and Georges Perec's 1965 novel _Things: A Story of the Sixties_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)
Though the posters display various styles, individual artists were never credited and each work was treated as the work of the collective.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)General assemblies were held to discuss and vote on the posters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-lat-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-eye-4) In a 1969 book of the posters, the _Atelier Populaire_ wrote "To use them for decorative purposes, to display them in bourgeois places of culture or to consider them as objects of aesthetic interest is to impair both their function and their effect."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)
Much of the imagery they created, including a poster of a truncheon-wielding riot policeman has since achieved iconic status.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3) The posters were rarely saved but were collected by Kugelberg who staged an exhibition at London's Hayward Gallery in 2008.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-ind-2) The exhibition commemorated the 40th anniversary of the protests.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-dd-1)

The book includes over 200 posters.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-int-6) As in the exhibition which preceded it, the posters in the book are accompanied by photographs taken by Vermés of the students, the production process and the protests,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-ind-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-eye-4) many of which were previously unpublished.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-int-6)
The book also includes a foreword by Vermés, a founder of the _Atelier Populaire_;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-ind-2) translations of first-hand accounts of students' and strikers' clashes with the police;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-int-6) manifestos and pamphlets;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-dd-1) a pictorial index, a bibliography, and a thumbnail gallery of posters that were not reproduced full-size.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-int-6)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-eye-4)
Writing in _The Guardian_, Justin McGuirk noted the continued relevance of "the spirit of '68" in the United Kingdom in the wake of the 2010 student protests, describing the book as "a beautiful volume". McGuirk questioned the absence of political design from the 2010 protests and occupations, as well as the commercial street art of Banksy and Shepard Fairey, and the contemporary popularity of the 1939 Keep Calm and Carry On poster.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-gu-3)

The _Los Angeles Times_'s Liesl Bradner also argued for the book's relevance in 2012 after the Occupy movement and _Time'_ s naming "the protester" as its Person of the Year in 2011.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-lat-5) Alex Bec of the art blog _It's Nice That_ noted that despite the events of May 1968 having been well documented, "_Beauty is in the Street_ blew everything before it out of the water."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-int-6) Fíacha O'Dubhda of _Eye_ described the book as one "that immerses the reader in the process through which spontaneous design and production were used to document, illustrate and instigate" the events of May 1968.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_in_the_Street#cite_note-eye-4)

Title: The Destruction of Bronze Statues in the Second World War
Chunks: 58,59,60
### Pantin
One of the largest French refineries was at Pantin, on the outskirts of Paris. Here, in 1941, photographer Pierre Jahan documented the last phase of the destruction of French bronze statues.
Learn more:
Pierre Jahan et Jean Cocteau, _La Mort et les statues_ (1946)
Kathryn Brown, "Remembering the Occupation: 'La Mort et les statues' by Pierre Jahan and Jean Cocteau" _Forum for Modern Language Studies_, 49:3 (July 2013): 286–299.

### Hamburg, Germany
The majority of French bronze statues were melted down in France between 1941 and late 1943, but some were transported intact to German refineries. The Zinnwerke Wilhelmsburg in Hamburg is said to have had “a great many bronze statues, some of tremendous size, and mostly broken.”[1]

On April 11, 2019, a crane lifted these sixteen copper statues off the spire of Notre-Dame for the first time in more than 150 years.

# Yes Yes Paris - On April 11, 2019, a crane lifted these... | Facebook
They represent the twelve apostles and the four evangelists, and they had stood at the base of the cathedral's spire since 1861, when architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc placed them there during his restoration of Notre-Dame. Standing 11 feet (3.4 meters) tall and weighing around 330 pounds (150 kilograms) each, they were finally coming down for a cleaning and restoration project that had been planned long before anyone imagined it would matter this much.
Four days later, on April 15, 2019, fire tore through the cathedral's roof and destroyed the spire itself. Had the statues still been up there, they would not have survived the heat.
Instead, they spent six years being restored at a workshop in Périgueux, in southwestern France, stripped of the green oxidation that had built up over more than a century and returned to their original chocolate brown color.
By the end of July 2025, all sixteen were back at the base of the rebuilt spire, exactly where Viollet-le-Duc had put them.

### Pantin
One of the largest French refineries was at Pantin, on the outskirts of Paris. Here, in 1941, photographer Pierre Jahan documented the last phase of the destruction of French bronze statues.
Learn more:
Pierre Jahan et Jean Cocteau, _La Mort et les statues_ (1946)
Kathryn Brown, "Remembering the Occupation: 'La Mort et les statues' by Pierre Jahan and Jean Cocteau" _Forum for Modern Language Studies_, 49:3 (July 2013): 286–299.

On April 11, 2019, a crane lifted these sixteen copper statues off the spire of Notre-Dame for the first time in more than 150 years.

# Yes Yes Paris - On April 11, 2019, a crane lifted these... | Facebook
They represent the twelve apostles and the four evangelists, and they had stood at the base of the cathedral's spire since 1861, when architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc placed them there during his restoration of Notre-Dame. Standing 11 feet (3.4 meters) tall and weighing around 330 pounds (150 kilograms) each, they were finally coming down for a cleaning and restoration project that had been planned long before anyone imagined it would matter this much.
Four days later, on April 15, 2019, fire tore through the cathedral's roof and destroyed the spire itself. Had the statues still been up there, they would not have survived the heat.
Instead, they spent six years being restored at a workshop in Périgueux, in southwestern France, stripped of the green oxidation that had built up over more than a century and returned to their original chocolate brown color.
By the end of July 2025, all sixteen were back at the base of the rebuilt spire, exactly where Viollet-le-Duc had put them.

Title: The Destruction of Bronze Statues in the Second World War
Chunks: 58,59,60
### Pantin
One of the largest French refineries was at Pantin, on the outskirts of Paris. Here, in 1941, photographer Pierre Jahan documented the last phase of the destruction of French bronze statues.
Learn more:
Pierre Jahan et Jean Cocteau, _La Mort et les statues_ (1946)
Kathryn Brown, "Remembering the Occupation: 'La Mort et les statues' by Pierre Jahan and Jean Cocteau" _Forum for Modern Language Studies_, 49:3 (July 2013): 286–299.

### Hamburg, Germany
The majority of French bronze statues were melted down in France between 1941 and late 1943, but some were transported intact to German refineries. The Zinnwerke Wilhelmsburg in Hamburg is said to have had “a great many bronze statues, some of tremendous size, and mostly broken.”[1]

### Pantin
One of the largest French refineries was at Pantin, on the outskirts of Paris. Here, in 1941, photographer Pierre Jahan documented the last phase of the destruction of French bronze statues.
Learn more:
Pierre Jahan et Jean Cocteau, _La Mort et les statues_ (1946)
Kathryn Brown, "Remembering the Occupation: 'La Mort et les statues' by Pierre Jahan and Jean Cocteau" _Forum for Modern Language Studies_, 49:3 (July 2013): 286–299.
texts.59:
### Hamburg, Germany
The majority of French bronze statues were melted down in France between 1941 and late 1943, but some were transported intact to German refineries. The Zinnwerke Wilhelmsburg in Hamburg is said to have had “a great many bronze statues, some of tremendous size, and mostly broken.”[1]
